## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kacchapajātaka* (Ja 273) is a story included in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the traditional opening blurb, the Buddha recounted this narrative while residing at Jetavana to address the reconciliation of a quarrel between two courtiers or magnates of the king of Kosala, noting that the introductory circumstances had previously been related in the Second Book. The verse incipit associated with the story is rendered as "Who is the one who brings the food".

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a Brahmin who practices austerities and enters deep meditation [Olson 2015]. The narrative features a disruptive, lascivious monkey who harasses the ascetic during contemplation and subsequently attempts to take sexual liberties with a tortoise sleeping by a riverbank [Olson 2015]. This work is one of several homonymous texts titled *Kacchapajātaka* in Pali literature, distinct from Ja 178 (the story of a tortoise attached to its drying pond) and Ja 215 (the talkative tortoise carried on a stick by geese) [Burlingame 1921; Anandajoti 2010; Olson 2015].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§2.4–3.4 ↔ §2364–2365)
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text-reuse database — Documents Pali-internal text reuse with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā and lack of external cross-language parallels.
- [Olson 2015] Carl Olson, Indian asceticism: Power, violence, and play (2015) — Summarizes the narrative content of Jātaka 273 involving the meditating ascetic, the monkey, and the tortoise.
- [Burlingame 1921] Eugene W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary (1921) — Clarifies homonymous Kacchapa Jātaka tales, specifically the talkative tortoise (Ja 215).
- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Ānandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses (2010) — Distinguishes Ja 178 Kacchapajātaka concerning non-attachment to home.
